Solution. Answer: 84. The overall average is:
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{20 \cdot 78+24 \cdot 89}{20+24} & =\frac{5 \cdot 78+6 \cdot 89}{5+6} \\ & =\frac{390+534}{11} \\ & =\frac{924}{11} \\ & =84 . \end{aligned} $$
Alternatively, since the overall average must be a bit more than 78, the overall average:
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{20 \cdot 78+24 \cdot 89}{20+24} & =\frac{(20+24) 78+24(89-78)}{20+24} \\ & =78+\frac{24 \cdot 11}{44} \\ & =78+6 \\ & =84 . \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q2.solution:
Solution. Answer: 15. Let $x$ be the height of the trunk still standing. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} XY=XY^{\prime} & =32-x \\ 64=8^{2} & =(32-x)^{2}-x^{2} \\ & =(32-x+x)(32-x-x) \\ & =32(32-2x) \\ \therefore 1 & =16-x \\ x & =16-1 \\ & =15 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q3.solution:
Solution. Answer: 7. We are given,
$$ \frac{3}{5} < \frac{n}{20} < \frac{3}{2} . $$
Clearing fractions by multiplying through by 20, we have,
$$ 12 < n < 30 . $$
So $n \in\{13,14, \ldots, 29\}$.
But $n / 20$ is a fraction in lowest terms, means that $\operatorname{gcd}(n, 20)=1$.
Thus, we must remove from $\{13, 14, \ldots, 29\}$ any numbers that are divisible by 2 or 5. This leaves,
$$ n \in\{13,17,19,21,23,27,29\}, $$
leaving 7 possibilities for $n$.

wajo26_q5.solution:
Solution. Answer: 11. The shortest possible number has 226 digits, since 225 digits can sum to at most $9\times225=2025$:
$$ 2026=9 \times 225+1 . $$
A leading digit of 1 forces all 225 other digits to be 9, giving the smallest number. The next smallest starts with 2. Its remaining digits must sum to 2024, one less than the maximum, so they are all 9 except for one 8. Put the 8 as early as possible to get $N=28\underbrace{99\ldots999}_{224\text{ 9s}}$.
$$ \therefore N+1=29 \underbrace{00 \ldots 000}_{224 \text { 0s }}, \text { whose digits sum to } 11 . $$

wajo26_q6.solution:
Solution. Answer: 30. Let $V$ be the volume of the sink in litres and let $r$ be the time taken for the right tap to fill the sink in minutes. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} V / 20, V / r & \text { are the L/min flow rates of } \\ & \text { the left and right taps, respectively. } \\ \therefore V & =\left(\frac{V}{20}+\frac{V}{r}\right) \cdot 12 \\ \therefore \frac{1}{12} & =\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{r} \\ \frac{1}{r} & =\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{20} \\ & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{15} \\ r & =2 \cdot 15 \\ & =30 \mathrm{~min} . \end{aligned} $$
Alternatively, let $V, r$ be defined as above.
Then the fractions of $V$ contributed by the left and right taps after 12 minutes are:
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{12}{20} & \text { and } \frac{12}{r}, \text { respectively. } \\ \therefore 1 & =\frac{12}{20}+\frac{12}{r} \\ & =\frac{3}{5}+\frac{12}{r} \\ \frac{2}{5} & =\frac{12}{r} \\ r & =\frac{12 \cdot 5}{2} \\ & =30 \mathrm{~min} . \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q8.solution:
Solution. Answer: 856. Let the other vertices of the rectangle be $B, C, D$ as shown.
Let $BM=MC=b$ and $CN=ND=a$. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} |ABCD| & =|ABM|+|MCN|+|ADN|+|AMN| \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2a \cdot b+\frac{1}{2} \cdot a \cdot b+\frac{1}{2} \cdot a \cdot 2b+321 \\ & =\frac{5}{2} \cdot ab+321 \\ \therefore \frac{3}{2} \cdot ab & =321 \\ |ABCD| & =4ab \\ & =4 \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot 321 \\ & =8 \cdot 107 \\ & =856 . \end{aligned} $$
First Alternative Solution: Let $O$ be the centre of the rectangle, with $a, b$ as above. Then each of $\triangle AOM, \triangle AON, \triangle MON$ has base and height $a, b$ in some order. So,
$$ \begin{aligned} 321=|AMN| & =|AOM|+|AON|+|MON| \\ & =\frac{3}{2} \cdot ab \\ & =\frac{3}{8}|ABCD| \\ \therefore|ABCD| & =\frac{8}{3} \cdot 321 \\ & =8 \cdot 107 \\ & =856 . \end{aligned} $$
Second Alternative solution: Let $S=|ABCD|$. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} 321=|AMN| & =|ABCD|-(|ABM|+|ADN|+|MNC|) \\ & =S-\left(\frac{1}{4} S+\frac{1}{4} S+\frac{1}{8} S\right) \\ & =\frac{3}{8} S \\ \therefore|ABCD|=S & =\frac{8}{3} \cdot 321 \\ & =8 \cdot 107 \\ & =856 . \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q11.solution:
Solution. Answer: 36. First observe that $M$ is the circumcentre of $\triangle ACL$, since $M$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AL$ of right triangle $ACL$.
Hence we have two isosceles triangles: $\triangle CMA$ and $\triangle PCB$.
Let $\alpha=\angle LAC=\frac{1}{2} \angle BAC$. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} \alpha & =\angle MAC \\ & =\angle MCA=\angle PCA \\ 90^{\circ}-2 \alpha & =\angle CBA \\ & =\angle CBP, \text { same angle } \\ & =\angle CPB, \triangle PCB \text { is isosceles } \\ & =\angle PCA+\angle PAC, \angle CPB \text { is ext. to } \triangle PCA \\ & =\alpha+2 \alpha \\ \therefore 90^{\circ} & =5 \alpha \\ \alpha & =18^{\circ} \\ \therefore \angle BAC & =2 \alpha \\ & =36^{\circ} . \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q12.solution:
Solution. Answer: 80. We need to find digits $x, y$ such that
$$ \overline{x 02 y}-\overline{2 x y 6} $$
is divisible by each of 2, 3 and 11 (since $66=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 11$ ).
Let a natural number $n$ have decimal digit representation $\overline{d_{k} \ldots d_{1} d_{0}}$, and define the following:
$S(n)$ is the sum of digits of $n$, i.e. $S(n)=d_{0}+d_{1}+\cdots+d_{k}$.
$A(n)$ is the alternating sum of digits of $n$, i.e. $A(n)=d_{0}-d_{1}+\cdots+(-1)^{k} d_{k}$.
Then the relevant rules regarding divisibility are:
Rule 2. $n$ is even, if $d_{0}$ is even.
Rule 3. $n$ and $S(n)$ have the same remainder when each is divided by 3.
Rule 11. $n$ and $A(n)$ have the same remainder when each is divided by 11.
By Rule 2., since $\overline{2 x y 6}$ is even, $\overline{x 02 y}$ must also be even. So $y$ is even.
By Rule 3., the difference of $S(\overline{2 x y 6})$ and $S(\overline{x 02 y})$ which is 6, must be divisible by 3.
Hmm! That doesn't tell us anything.
And, by Rule 11., the difference of $A(\overline{2 x y 6})$ and $A(\overline{x 02 y})$, must be divisible by 11. But,
$$ \begin{aligned} A(\overline{x 02 y})-A(\overline{2 x y 6}) & =(y-2+0-x)-(6-y+x-2) \\ & =2 y-2 x-6 \\ & =2(y-x-3) \end{aligned} $$
being divisible by 11, implies $y-x-3$ is divisible by 11, where
$$ -12 \leqslant y-x-3 \leqslant 6 $$
(The extreme values of $y-x-3$ occur for $y=0$ and $x=9$, and for $y=9$ and $x=0$, respectively.)
So, either $y-x-3=-11$ or $y-x-3=0$, i.e. $x=y+8$ or $x=y-3$ with $y$ even.
Since we want the largest possible $\overline{x y}$, we want $x$ as large as possible, which must occur with $x=8$ and $y=0$, i.e. largest $\overline{x y}=80$.
Tabulating all the possibilities, we have:
$$ \begin{array}{cccc} y & x=y-3 & x=y+8 & \overline{x y} \\ 0 & -3 & 8 & 80 \\ 2 & -1 & 10 & - \\ 4 & 1 & 12 & 14 \\ 6 & 3 & 14 & 36 \\ 8 & 5 & 16 & 58 \end{array} $$
So there are 4 possibilities for $\overline{x y}$, the largest of which is 80.

wajo26_q13.solution:
Solution. Answer: 26. We have,
$$ \begin{aligned} 45^{2}+a^{2} & =a+b+a b+a^{2}=(a+b)(1+a) \\ 45^{2}+b^{2} & =a+b+a b+b^{2}=(a+b)(1+b) \\ \therefore M & =\frac{\left(45^{2}+a^{2}\right)\left(45^{2}+b^{2}\right)}{(a+b)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{(a+b)(1+a)(a+b)(1+b)}{(a+b)^{2}} \\ & =(1+a)(1+b) \\ & =1+a+b+a b \\ & =1+45^{2} \\ & =2026, \end{aligned} $$
which leaves remainder 26, on division by 1000.

wajo26_q14.solution:
Solution. Answer: 144. Let $P$ be the point on $BC$ such that $GP\parallel AB$, and write $x$ for the side length of the square. The horizontal distance from $G$ to $H$ is $GP=x$. The vertical distance from $E$ to $F$ is also $x$, since they lie on the lines of opposite sides.
The right triangle formed by the horizontal and vertical displacements along $EF$ is similar to $\triangle GPH$. Their hypotenuses are $EF=2+15+3=20$ and $GH=15$. Thus $HP=(15/20)x=3x/4$. The legs $HP$ and $GP$ are in the ratio $3:4$, so $\triangle GPH$ is a $3:4:5$ right triangle.
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore x & =\frac{4}{5} \cdot 15 \\ & =12 \\ \therefore|ABCD| & =x^{2} \\ & =12^{2} \\ & =144 . \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q15.solution:
Solution. Answer: 336. Let $S, B$ be the sets of swimmers and bicyclists, respectively.
Let $y=\left|(S \cup B)^{\prime}\right|$, (the number of students who could neither swim nor ride)
$$ x=|S \cup B|, \quad \text { (the number of students who could ride or swim) } $$
Note that $x$ is the number of "remaining students", referred to in (i).
$$ \begin{array}{rlrl} |B| & =\frac{5}{7} x, & & \text { by (i) } \\ |S \backslash B| & =\frac{2}{7} x, & & \text { no. who can swim but not cycle } \\ |S \cap B| & =\frac{2}{9} \cdot|B|, & & \text { by (ii) } \\ & =\frac{2}{9} \cdot \frac{5}{7} x & & \\ & =\frac{10}{63} x & & \\ |B \backslash S| & =\frac{7}{9} \cdot \frac{5}{7} x, & & \text { no. who can cycle but not swim } \\ & =\frac{5}{9} x & & \\ x+y & =\text { no. of students surveyed } & \text { by (iii) } \\ \frac{5}{12}(x+y) & =|S|, & & =|S \backslash B|+|S \cap B| \\ & =\frac{2}{7} x+\frac{2}{9} \cdot \frac{5}{7} x & \\ & =\frac{2}{7} x\left(1+\frac{5}{9}\right) & \\ & =\frac{2}{7} \cdot \frac{14}{9} x & \\ & =\frac{4}{9} x & \\ \therefore \frac{5}{12} y & =\left(\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{12}\right) x & & \\ y & =\frac{12}{5}\left(\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{12}\right) x & & \\ & =\frac{x}{15} & & \end{array} $$
Now $x$ is the least integer such that $\frac{1}{15} x, \frac{2}{7} x, \frac{10}{63} x, \frac{5}{9} x$ are all integers, i.e.
$$ \begin{aligned} x & =\operatorname{lcm}(15,7,63,9) \\ & =\operatorname{lcm}(5,63) \\ & =315 \\ \therefore x+y & =x+\frac{1}{15} x \\ & =315+\frac{1}{15} \cdot 315 \\ & =315+21 \\ & =336 . \end{aligned} $$

wajo26_q16.solution:
Solution. Answer: 72. First we must find $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$ \begin{aligned} m^{2} & =n(n+2026) \\ & =n^{2}+2026 n \\ \therefore m^{2}+1013^{2} & =n^{2}+2026 n+1013^{2}, \text { completing the square } \\ & =(n+1013)^{2} \\ 1013^{2} & =(n+1013)^{2}-m^{2} \\ & =(n+1013+m)(n+1013-m) \quad(*) \end{aligned} $$
Now 1013 is prime, so there are exactly two ways (up to order) to write $1013^{2}$ as the product of two positive factors:
$$ 1013^{2}=1013 \cdot 1013 \text { and } 1013^{2}=1013^{2} \cdot 1 . $$
So $(*)$ gives us two cases:
Case 1: $n+1013+m=1013=n+1013-m$.
In this case, $n=m=0$ ( $n$ should be positive).
Case 2: $n+1013+m=1013^{2}, n+1013-m=1$. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} n+m & =1013^{2}-1013, & & (1)\\ n-m & =1-1013, & & (2)\\ \therefore n & =\frac{1}{2}\left(1013^{2}+1\right)-1013, & & \frac{1}{2}((1)+(2)) \\ m & =\frac{1}{2}\left(1013^{2}-1\right), & & \frac{1}{2}((1)-(2)) \end{aligned} $$
So there is only one solution to the problem.
Therefore,
$$ \begin{aligned} S=n & =\frac{1}{2}\left(1013^{2}+1\right)-1013 \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left(1000^{2}+2 \cdot 13 \cdot 1000+13^{2}+1\right)-1000-13 \\ & =1000(500+13-1)+\frac{1}{2}\left(13^{2}+1\right)-13 \\ & =1000(500+13-1)+85-13 \\ & =1000 \cdot 512+72 \end{aligned} $$
which on division by 1000 leaves remainder 72.
Alternatively, with $m$ as above, we start by writing $n=a^{2} x$, where $x$ is square-free (i.e. $x$ is the product of distinct prime factors, or $x=1$ ):
$$ \begin{aligned} m^{2} & =n(n+2026) \\ & =a^{2} x\left(a^{2} x+2026\right) \\ \therefore a^{2} x+2026 & =b^{2} x, \text { for some } b \in \mathbb{N}(\text { and } m=abx) \\ 2026 & =\left(b^{2}-a^{2}\right) x \\ & =(b+a)(b-a) x . \end{aligned} $$
Now, $2026=2 \cdot 1013$, where 1013 is prime, and $b+a$ and $b-a$ have the same parity. But $b+a$ and $b-a$ can't both be even (2026 is not divisible by 4).
So $b+a$ and $b-a$ are both odd, leaving $x$ even, i.e. $x=2026$ or $x=2$.
But $x=2026$, makes $b+a=b-a=1$, leading to $a=0$, whence $n=0$.
This leaves just the one possibility: $x=2$ and
$$ \begin{aligned} b+a & =1013 \\ b-a & =1 \\ \therefore a & =\frac{1}{2}(1013-1) \\ & =506 \end{aligned} $$
$S=n=a^{2} x$, (only one possibility for $n$ implies $S=n$ )
$$ \begin{aligned} & =506^{2} \cdot 2 \\ & =1012 \cdot 506 \\ & =1000 \cdot 506+12 \cdot 500+12 \cdot 6 \\ & =1000 \cdot 512+72 \end{aligned} $$
which on division by 1000 leaves remainder 72.
